one_line_description.value: Close is a CRM with calling, email, SMS, automation, and AI built in for sales teams.
one_line_description.quote: Calling, email, SMS, automation, and AI are built in, so your team can reach more leads, follow up faster, and close more deals.

has_public_api.quote: Whether you're a Close customer automating your sales process or a partner building an integration, the Close Developer Platform gives everything you or your AI agents need.

api_type.quote: Close uses industry-standard REST conventions with predictable URL structures, standard HTTP methods, and JSON request/response bodies.

api_breadth.value: REST/JSON, read-write across leads, contacts, opportunities, activities, custom fields, tasks, webhooks, and a 30-day event log; endpoint count not published
api_breadth.quote: Push leads, contacts, activities, and custom data into Close from your website or other systems via the REST API.

docs_url.quote: Full endpoint docs with schemas, examples, and an interactive API explorer.

auth_methods.quote: - API Keys — Best for scripts, internal tools, and server-side integrations. Use HTTP Basic Auth with your API key as the username and an empty password. - OAuth 2.0 — Best for user-facing integrations.

oauth_scopes_documented.quote: If your application has `offline_access` scope `refresh_token` property will be present in the response and you can refresh Access Token (See below).

access_model.quote: API keys can be created and managed in your Close account under Settings → Developer → API Keys.

access_notes.value: API keys are generated self-serve from an existing Close account (Settings → Developer → API Keys) scoped to a user/organization; API keys suit internal scripts while OAuth 2.0 apps are the route for third-party integrations. No sales contact, partner approval, or app review is documented, but no pricing page or free developer tier was captured, so a paid Close subscription may be required before keys can be minted.
access_notes.quote: API keys are best used for scripts and simple integrations that are internal to your organization. Alternatively, see Authentication with OAuth instead.

official_mcp_server.quote: The MCP server URL is `https://mcp.close.com/mcp` and has "HTTP Streamable" and "OAuth 2.0 Dynamic Client Registration (DCR)" support.

rate_limits.value: Per endpoint group, enforced per API key and per organization (org limit is 3x the API key limit); example 20 RPS per API key / 60 RPS per organization; 429 responses include RateLimit and retry-after headers
rate_limits.quote: if the API key rate limit maximum requests per second (RPS) is 20 RPS, the organization wide limit would be 60 RPS for that same endpoint group.

webhooks.quote: Webhooks — Subscribe to events and receive POST notifications when data changes.

sdk_languages.quote: Community libraries for Python, Node.js, Ruby, PHP, Go, and more.

api_versioning_or_deprecation_notes.value: Versioned base URL https://api.close.com/api/v1; an API changelog publishes updates and deprecations; no formal versioning/sunset policy text was captured in the evidence
api_versioning_or_deprecation_notes.quote: API Changelog — Latest API updates and deprecations.

verdict_reason: Close documents a broad REST API (base https://api.close.com/api/v1) with API-key/Basic auth and OAuth 2.0, webhooks, a 30-day event log, and an official MCP server at https://mcp.close.com/mcp. Credentials are self-serve from inside a Close account, with no partner approval or app review documented for API keys. The remaining gate is that an existing Close account/subscription appears necessary to mint API keys, and no free developer tier or pricing evidence was captured, so this lands at moderate rather than easy.
main_blocker: Requires an existing Close account/subscription to create API keys (no free developer tier evidenced)
open_questions: Pricing page was never captured (pricing search returned only partners.close.com and a glossary page); whether Close offers a free trial or free developer edition permitting API key creation is unevidenced, so access_model is medium confidence.

No documented sandbox/test environment appears in the fetched sources; help.close.com's secondary-organization page was indexed for the sandbox query but not fetched, so sandbox_or_test_env is left not_found.
Full OAuth scope list was not captured; only all.full_access and offline_access appear in token examples, so scope granularity/permission model is unverified.
The API changelog/versioning pages were indexed but not fetched, so any formal deprecation/sunset timeline or version-negotiation scheme is unverified.
No official vendor SDKs were found; the API Clients page lists only community libraries, so sdk_languages is recorded as an empty list.
No endpoint/resource count is published in the fetched documentation, so api_breadth is qualitative rather than numeric.
No community/third-party MCP servers were found in the provided registry or GitHub checks; community_mcp_servers is not_found rather than an asserted empty list.
